title: Scoop: Trump tells Max Miller his candidacy is in trouble
description: President Trump phoned Rep. Max Miller Monday and expressed doubts about the Ohio Republican's candidacy amid reports he assaulted his ex-wife and their child, three sources familiar with the call said. On the call, the president told Miller that "things aren't looking good" and repeatedly said his reelection would be tough, the three sources said. Miller, who denies hurting his wife and child, told the president he is staying in the race, one of the sources said. Miller said his own polling showed him in solid shape. Why it matters : The Monday night private conversation was different in tone than Trump's public comments about Miller. The president has refrained from criticizing Miller or from calling on him to drop out of his race. Miller, a former Trump White House aide, was married in 2022 to Emily Moreno, the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, at Trump's golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey. Later that year, Miller was elected to Ohio's 7th congressional district and was endorsed by Trump. He's in a competitive race for reelection this fall. In 2024, Miller and his ex-wife split up prior to their divorce. Earlier Monday, Trump did not back away from Miller, calling the situation "a very sad thing." "I know Max, he's a good person, I mean I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out," Trump said. "It's accusations. And I'm going to let them figure that out." A White House spokesperson and a spokesperson for Miller declined to comment.

title: Exclusive: House Democratic Women's Caucus calls on Chuck Edwards to resign
description: The House Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) to resign after the House Ethics Committee concluded he violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment, according to a statement shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is arguing that censure — the punishment recommended by the bipartisan Ethics Committee — is not sufficient for Edwards. "A censure has no real consequences," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (Mich.) wrote in a statement obtained by Axios. As part of the bipartisan sexual misconduct task force , they also plan to introduce legislation creating tougher penalties for lawmakers found to have committed sexual misconduct, including stripping committee assignments or requiring an expulsion vote. Edwards did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the call for his resignation. "It just means he has to stand on the floor of the House while the censure is read. A few minutes of embarrassing C-SPAN coverage, while the staffers themselves had to endure over two years of sexual harassment, is not comparable." Edwards did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the Ethics Committee's findings. But in a statement to the committee, Edwards' attorneys said the panel cleared him of sexual misconduct and quid pro quo harassment, arguing it improperly recommended censure based on vague House conduct standards rather than any direct violation of sexual harassment rules. Driving the news: The House Ethics Committee found Edwards violated House rules by "failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers," according to a 25-page report released Monday. The report's findings confirmed several incidents previously reported by Axios , including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. "The report released by the House Committee on Ethics detailing their investigation into Rep. Chuck Edwards showed a clear and outlandish pattern of sexual harassment. It's time for accountability. There must be clear and significant consequences for sexual harassment of this level," the lawmakers wrote. Zoom in: Democratic Women's Caucus leaders argued Edwards' conduct drove two staffers from their jobs and warranted consequences beyond censure. "They had to leave their jobs, so should Rep. Edwards. He should resign immediately," they wrote. "Congress has a responsibility to protect the women that work here and reciting a few words of censure on the House floor doesn't protect women from retaliation and sexual harassment." What's next: The House is expected to vote on censuring Edwards after returning from the August recess, and Republicans already say the outcome is all but certain. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) told Axios she will vote to censure Edwards. "Sexual harassment is completely unacceptable," Luna said. A House GOP leadership aide told Axios they "don't see a path" where Edwards avoids censure.

title: Blanche poised for confirmation vote after he kills Trump's fund
description: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche will likely advance to a full Senate confirmation vote after he rescinded the order setting up President Trump's $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund Sunday. Why it matters: Blanche's Sunday order has won over Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who had held out on voting for Trump's pick. State of play: Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement that they will vote to advance Blanche's nomination. The senators said they had negotiated a "legally enforceable document" that ends the anti-weaponization fund and limits protections against audits. "We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon," the senators said in the statement. What they're saying: A Department of Justice spokesperson did not directly answer Axios' questions about whether Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization had agreed in writing to rescind the fund. Instead, the spokesperson pointed to Blanche's Aug. 2 order rescinding the fund and to Blanche's earlier testimony that the May 19 order "has effect only on plaintiffs and defendants, and that the release is retroactive only." Catch up quick: The fund grew out of a May settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over the disclosure of his tax records. The settlement promised an apology to Trump and his sons, and it created the fund for individuals claiming they suffered from government "lawfare." Another agreement released Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from certain IRS claims and audits. Of note: Blanche's new order rescinds one from May implementing the nearly $1.8 billion fund, but not the settlement provision requiring the attorney general to create the fund. The settlement's terms can be changed only via a written agreement from the Trumps and the government. Sunday's order was signed by Blanche but not by Trump, his sons or the Trump Organization. At his hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee last month, Blanche acknowledged that the settlement was enforceable and that Trump's lawyers could try to enforce it or claim the DOJ breached the agreement by refusing to operate the fund. On Sunday, Blanche also clarified the sweeping protections Trump received from tax audits. In a statement released with the order, Blanche said the protections apply only retroactively and only to the lawsuit's named plaintiffs: Trump, some of his family, and the Trump Organization. The earlier agreement said it extended to any "related or affiliated" individuals, companies and other organizations. Reality check: While the Trump protections Blanche listed are without precedent, they also reflect the reality that Trump's administration will not criminally investigate him in any way. Before he leaves office, Trump is expected to hand out sweeping pardons to administration officials and allies. That would render any effort to prosecute Trump, his family or his companies doubly moot. Friction point: Trump complicated the negotiations Saturday when he threatened to keep Blanche as acting attorney general and revive the fund. "It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote. Flashback: U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams found that Trump's initial lawsuit was brought to manipulate the judicial process since Trump controlled both sides of the litigation. She stopped short of deciding if the agreement was enforceable as a private contract. U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema barred the DOJ from operating the fund, but she said she'd likely dismiss that case if top officials killed the fund. U.S. District Judge Richard Leon reached a different result in a separate case, declining to block the fund since the DOJ had said it was not moving forward. What's next: The Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled a vote on Tuesday. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.
